extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and critics interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on balancing pictorial scene-setting and dramatic action in novels — how to use background, description, viewpoint, and time-compression to support credible drama. Focuses on methods exemplified by Balzac, Dickens, Stevenson and Thackeray.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized picture as propulsive force
rubrics_metrics.description: “The effect of the generalized picture, for example, supporting the play of action, is one in which Balzac particularly delights... It becomes more than a support, it becomes a kind of propulsive force applied to the action at the start.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a richly rendered background or generalized picture to store up a reserve of energy that can drive the drama when it begins. Examples: Le Curé de Village, Père Goriot, La Recherche de l’Absolu, Eugénie Grandet. The picture should be prepared in advance so that when the story proper starts, the action inherits that force without needing further setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat setting as equally important as events
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nobody gives such attention as Balzac does... to the setting of the scene; he clearly considers these preparatory pictures quite as important as the events which they are to enclose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the scene (towns, houses, workshops) as material that provides character and energy to the drama. Good setting does not merely decorate; it supplies motivations, associations and credibility that the events can draw on. Example: Maison Vauquer in Père Goriot supplies ‘the daily experience of the dingy house’ to Goriot’s actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of scene — create scene to provide future dramatic force
rubrics_metrics.description: “Balzac’s care in creating the scene, therefore, is truly economical; it is not merely a manner of setting the stage for the drama, it is a provision of character and energy for the drama when it begins.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build scenes with economy—include details that will later function in the drama rather than extraneous decoration. Prepare ‘dormant echoes’ in the scene that will be awakened by later events so that even a slight plot can feel weighty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed factual description vs impressionism — know your image
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac sometimes appears “possessed by the lust of description for its own sake... an insatiable desire to put every detail in its place,” yet because “he more than anyone else, knows everything,” he can reproduce the scene “inch by inch” without losing the whole impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use exhaustive, inventory-like description, only do so if you genuinely possess the full image in mind; otherwise the result becomes mechanical and tiresome. Anti-pattern: piling up facts when the writer lacks the unifying vision—this produces detail that 'tells us nothing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression of experience into short form
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nobody knows how to compress so much experience into two or three hundred pages as Balzac did unfailingly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn how to make each scene and detail carry maximum narrative weight so that a large sweep of life can be rendered in a brief novel. This is achieved by concentrating salient facts and by using setting and accumulated background to imply wider experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recurring/overlapping characters — unity vs mechanical intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac’s device of making characters overlap across books may give the Comédie a look of unity, but it can be 'less artistic and more mechanical' and may not enhance a single story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when reusing characters across works: while it can suggest a larger world, background knowledge about an incidental character may be irrelevant (or distracting) to the foreground story. Only let recurring figures carry past associations if those associations serve the immediate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background figures must shed irrelevant life in specific stories
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of the characters in the remoter planes of the action... no more is expected than their value for the purpose of the action in the foreground. That is all that can be used in the book; whatever more they may bring will lie idle, will contribute nothing, and may even become an embarrassment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a previously known character appears incidentally, strip away irrelevant backstory so they function cleanly within the present plot. Leaving idle associations visible risks confusing the story’s unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial method to subdue extravagant drama
rubrics_metrics.description: “Where the action... is likely to seem harsh, overcharged, romantic, it is made to look less so, less hazardous and more real, by recourse to the art of the picture-maker.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your plot tends toward melodrama or improbability, use careful scene-setting and pictorial detail to qualify and temper the dramatic action, thereby making it more credible to the reader. This is a deliberate reversal: use picture to rescue drama from seeming violent or incredible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of mixing glaring romance with sober truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac’s passion for truth was often in conflict with his lust for marvels; when romance is 'gaudy' it remains glaringly false against a background of sober fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either moderate the romance so it can be absorbed by the realistic background, or avoid such sharp contrasts. Success depends on the imaginative merging of truth and romance; where they remain sharply distinct, the method fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual introduction of romantic drama through populated scenes (Dickensian method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stevenson noted how Dickens’s way was “to lead gradually into [romantic intrigues], through well-populated scenes of character and humour; so that his world is actual... by the time that his plot begins to thicken.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate the prelude with vivid characters and humour so that when the dramatic or romantic core arrives it is already plausible. Use a broad, diverse picture that slowly narrows into focused action (examples: Bleak House, Dombey and Son, Our Mutual Friend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer action/dialogue or general narrative according to authorial strength
rubrics_metrics.description: “Dickens continually holds to the immediate scene... he is always readier to work in action and dialogue than to describe at large; he is happier in placing a character there before us... than in reflecting a long impression.” In contrast Thackeray often uses far-seeing narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a presentational method aligned with your strengths: if you excel at dramatic scenes and dialogue, render your 'picture' as incident and specific occasions; if you prefer reflective, far-seeing narration, you may summarize and linger on broader impressions. Don’t force a method unsuited to the material or your voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallized characterization for dramatized presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Dickens presents his picture as action, he is “forced to crystallize and formulate his characters very sharply,” often reducing them to a trick or a phrase which they bring each time they appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on brief scenes to convey character, sharpen defining traits so they register quickly; labelling or emblematic devices can be effective but are exigent—they risk caricature if overused. Ensure each recurring trait serves the dramatic necessity of the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person narration as a tool to tone drama or enhance picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Rendering events 'as somebody’s narrative' can either 'work the drama into a picture' or push the book toward a pictured impression, depending on subject and use (Stevenson’s use of first person discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider first-person narration when you want to filter dramatic events through a witness’s perspective: it can qualify or distance action, creating either greater credibility or a specific pictorial gloss. Match the narrating voice to the effect you intend (e.g., Esmond vs The Master of Ballantrae).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using scene and preparatory picture to convey long durations economically
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac can state casually, ‘Five years went by in this way,’ yet still make the fading of hope appear gradual because his prepared picture provides a 'complete and enduring impression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To render long spans of time without exhaustive interior narration, prepare an authoritative, detailed scene and social context beforehand; the reader will then accept summary leaps in time because the background supplies the sense of duration. Anti-pattern: assuming a mere statement of elapsed time will suffice without a rich pre-established scene.
